CNBC Exclusive: Transcript: Pershing Square Founder & CEO Bill Ackman Speaks with CNBC’s Sara Eisen on “Squawk on the Street” Today

# CNBC Exclusive: Transcript: Pershing Square Founder & CEO Bill Ackman Speaks with CNBC’s Sara Eisen on “Squawk on the Street” Today

Published Thu, Oct 22 2026 1:20 PM EDT

WHEN: Today, Thursday, October 22, 2026

WHERE: CNBC's "Squawk on the Street"

Following is the unofficial transcript of a CNBC exclusive interview with Pershing Square Founder & CEO Bill Ackman on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" (M-F, 9AM-12PM ET) today, Thursday, October 22. Following are links to video on CNBC.com: https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/22/bill-ackman-says-2027-will-be-an-amazing-year-for-stocks.html, https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/22/bill-ackman-on-fannie-and-freddie.html, https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/22/bill-ackman-iran-war-has-been-extremely-well-executed.html, https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/22/bill-ackman-meta-is-incredibly-undervalued.html, and https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/22/bill-ackman-netflix-is-a-high-growth-utility.html.

All references must be sourced to CNBC.

SARA EISEN: Next Tuesday, Israelis will be casting votes for prime minister in what is widely expected to be a close and heated election. It's the first national election in Israel since the October 7 terrorist attack in 2023. Meantime, U.S. midterm elections set to take place the following week, as U.S. support for Israel has become an increasingly divisive issue. Amid all the politics and geopolitical noise, though, money has been flowing into Israel at record levels. The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, for instance, has tripled in three years. And foreign direct inflows into Israel were up 78 percent in 2025 from the year before; $26.2 billion is the number versus almost $15 billion in '24. One of those investors is famed hedge fund manager and CEO of Pershing Square Capital Bill Ackman. He is in Israel right now and joins us exclusively from the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, where he is a partial owner of the exchange. Bill, it's so great to have you from Israel. I understand you're there. You're, you've been speaking at a conference on healthcare innovation. What has you attracted right now to what you're seeing there?

BILL ACKMAN: So, I think it's one of the most innovative economies in the world. It's also one of the best economies in the world. If you look at their kind of overall macro statistics, growth expected to be 7.5%, meanwhile, inflation is very low. Currency is strong. It's an, overall, sovereign debt is relatively low. So it's a very well-run economy. It's one of the most innovative economies in the world. You might have heard of our Pershing Square Ventures. We mentioned our last quarter, we are going to be investing, we have been investing in some kind of pre-IPO and earlier stage companies. This is actually a pretty good place to find some of them. So that's among other reasons why I'm here.

EISEN: I mean, you are standing at the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, Bill, where you invested and bought an almost 5 percent stake just a few months after October 7. It was such a dark time for Israel. The investment has returned ninefold since then. It's got to be one of your best investments. What did you see that other people didn't?

ACKMAN: Well, it was, obviously, when they say there's blood in the streets, it's usually, unfortunately, an opportunistic time to invest. I'm a big believer in the country long term. It's one of the highest ratios, as I say, sort of I.Q. and I.P. per capita. Israel, one of its biggest competitive disadvantages is the small size of the country. I would say that's becoming a competitive advantage. The larger countries with big sort of welfare state, you look at what's going on in France right now. Being a smaller country with a ton of innovation and an environment that's very favorable for start-ups, and also just if you think about the grit of a people that have been through a several-year war, you have got an entire generation of talent. War is a great place to learn about leadership, develop grit. And, also, Israel's very well-known for the technology training that happens. So you have all these start-ups being led. You have all the big venture firms here, Sequoia and others opening up offices, so that all these things are going to drive the Israeli economy.

EISEN: Yes, I was just going to ask you for, if you're speaking to investors who are wondering if they should have more exposure to Israel in their portfolios, but are worried about the never-ending war and increasing geopolitical risk and backlash from around the world, divestment policies and that sort of thing. I mean, how do you, how do you square some of those risks with the opportunities that you see?

ACKMAN: Yes, I think investors are actually, most investors are pretty apolitical. They want to invest their capital where they're going to earn an attractive return. This is a very good place to put your money. It's an incredibly resilient country. You know, it's, the way I describe it, imagine if Silicon Valley was a country, and that's Israel.

EISEN: Yeah.

ACKMAN: And so I think it's going to do very well. It's now a, from the exchange's perspective, it used to have a sort of an off-sequence exchange. It's now a Monday-to-Friday exchange, as opposed to Sunday to Thursday. It will get added to more kind of global indices over time. The market's up a ton without the addition to some of these global indices. That's also going to be a big driver over time. I think you're also going to see a lot of, there's so many start-ups being formed here. Nasdaq, New York Stock Exchange eligibility, you won't get noticed these days unless you're of pretty significant scale, whereas, in the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, you can have significant market exposure. So I think a lot of companies will list here first, and then, if you will, graduate and have a dual listing in the U.S. So, I'm a big, big fan of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange and the country generally. I'm married to an Israeli, of course, which also gave me sort of the inside scoop.

EISEN: Yes, so it's personal. And what about the election, Bill, that's coming up next week? How critical is it to the thesis?

ACKMAN: You know, I think the country's going to do very well regardless of who is selected as prime minister. And I do think the country will do better if there's less divisiveness, I would say a bit like our country. I think political divisiveness has not been good for Israel. It's not been good for our country. I think the ideal scenario is that there's a broad coalition that works for the benefit of the country as a whole, as opposed to a very narrow victory by one party, one candidate. You know, again, a world in which there's a decisive election is much better than a world in which there's a close election.

EISEN: What about, I mean, there's this report from "The New York Times" that war will begin again after the midterm elections with Iran. When we talked last, I think it was in May at the Milken Conference, you sounded very supportive of the strikes on Iran. And I wonder what you make now of the current strategy and where you think this is all going.

ACKMAN: Look, I think Iran has been a grave threat to the U.S. and to the world. I think you have a radical leadership that gets control of nuclear weapons, and that is really existential for the world. So I think the president did absolutely the right thing in really diminishing Iran's nuclear capability. The job is not quite finished. I think he wants to finish the job. I think that is important for the world. The consequence, no one likes. No one likes higher energy prices. No one likes higher gas prices. But I think we have to look at this on a longer-term basis. And, again, once the overhang of the war is done, and if it sounds like we're also potentially heading in the right direction on Russia-Ukraine, energy prices could come way down. And, obviously, that would be very, very good for inflation and for markets. I would say Iran and Russia-Ukraine are sort of one, two things holding the, I mean, what is still a very booming kind of market environment. You get those out of the way, inflation comes down, rates come down, you're going to have, we're going to have an amazing 2027. So, obviously, the president wants to resolve this war, but wants to, this is, the IRGC killed 85,000 or so, whatever the recent estimates are, of people protesting the government. It's a very evil and dangerous regime that's been stirring up a big mess in the Middle East. I think there will be a massive peace dividend resolving this. I think the Abraham Accords will expand. It'll be great for Saudi Arabia, great for UAE, great for the region, great for Israel, and ultimately great for the United States. So I think it's been an extremely well executed war with relatively minimal—

EISEN: You do?

ACKMAN: You know, obviously, every casualty is a tragic one. Yes, it's extremely well executed, absolutely. Now, the IRGC is, it's very difficult to rid a radical group, but they have been dismantled to an amazing extent, no real air capability, no navy—

EISEN: Yeah.

ACKMAN: And less and less limited capability in terms of fighting war. So, I think it's been going well, very well done.

EISEN: But it's not popular in the U.S., you know? It's not popular in the U.S. And we're looking at, we're going into the midterms and—

ACKMAN: Well, I think we're too—

EISEN: Go ahead.

ACKMAN: I hear you. And, look, credit to the president that he's prepared to do what's right for the country long term, even though it may have shorter-term political consequences. I think you want a president that does what's right for America on a long-term basis, as opposed to, the politicians I object to are the ones that say or do things or support candidates because it's important for their getting reelected. That's how we end up with the wrong people in power. Running the country, we should be making, the Chinese are well-known for making decisions on a generational, some people say century-type basis. We need, we need to make smart decisions. We can't let a nuclear power emerge with this evil leadership.

EISEN: Given where the politics are in this country, where do you think the U.S.-Israel relationship goes from here?

ACKMAN: Look, I think that, once this war is out of the way, it will depend to some degree on who, what the next leadership of Israel is going to be, what the nature of a coalition kind of looks like. But I think I think the, Israel has proven itself a very important ally in this region. We could, it would have been a lot riskier for us to take out, the B-2 takeout of Fordow and otherwise happened after Israel took out most of Iran's air defense capability, so that, the secretary of war has been very effusive about that partnership. And Israel is one of the most capable militaries in the world. And having Israel onside in this very challenged region, I think, has been a very important thing for U.S. supremacy.

EISEN: Yes. But And yet we have a Senate candidate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, who said this week Israel is not actually our friend. And more and more people seem to be behind him.

ACKMAN: Yes.

EISEN: He's up in the polls. How did this go wrong? And how does it, does it turn? Does it turn around?

ACKMAN: Look, that's a, I'm not a fan of, more and more evidence is coming out that his family and he are, have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which is an avowed terrorist organization. The notion that a person, a person of that ilk is going to be, is a candidate for the Senate and has a shot of winning is, I would say, deeply concerning and should be for every American.

EISEN: What does the second half look like overall to you if the Dems do sweep in the midterms?

ACKMAN: You know, more challenging for the president to get things done. Look, I think President Trump is very focused on his, I'm sure his goal is to be the greatest president ever, in his own words. He will be focused on his legacy. But I would say he will be unbound by short-term political considerations. He could continue to do what's right for the country on a long-term basis.

EISEN: I also want to ask you, Bill, while we have you, of course, about your portfolio. The fund is down this year in an up market. So what do you, what do you tell shareholders about why that is and what you think of the valuation and why they should stick with it?

ACKMAN: Sure. Yes. So our goal is not to find stocks that are going to go up in the next 90 days. The market has increasingly moved to a very short-term dynamic. Index funds are forever holders, but effectively taking stocks out of the float, and then very short-term investors trying to estimate whether a company's going to make or miss earnings or guidance, and that, it led to like massive market volatility. And the focus this year has been on AI-adjacent sort of hardware, energy very narrow market. And that's really created what we think is a great opportunity for us over a multi-year period of time to buy some of the great franchise, durable growth companies we have loved, always wanted to own, but they were at kind of going in earnings yields or P/E multiples that made them, the kind of go-forward return, less attractive for us. And we have been able to buy businesses, Visa, Mastercard, Netflix, and others at prices that we pencil out to well north of 20 percent IRRs over three-, four-, five-year holding periods. So it's a great setup for us. Of course, we'd love to finish the year strong. Every investment manager wants to have a positive year. We do have some, if our money could leave every day or every month or at the end of the year, we would probably try to position the portfolio differently, but I think that would lead to suboptimal longer-term returns. So we feel we're down modestly, single digits for our largest fund. And for our new vehicle, we're actually, well, before I got to Israel, we were up slightly from launch over a small period of time.

EISEN: Yes.

ACKMAN: But, most importantly, we deployed $5 billion of capital of Pershing Square USA in some very high-quality long-term durable compounders that are less, I would say, sexy for people trying to make money next month, but I think will, they will continue to compound their earnings and grow at very high rates over time.

EISEN: Well, since you mentioned Netflix, that was one that I wanted to ask you about, because the company reported yesterday. And it was pretty disappointing, capping off a kind of ugly performance for Netflix with some real questions about how long it could take to revive their content slate, what the competition looks like, engagement. Why, I think you added it back as of the August filing. What's the, what's your, what's your expectation there?

ACKMAN: Yes. Actually, so, I was on the plane when the, when the earnings kind of came out. I had a brief opportunity to get an update from the team. We actually viewed the quarter very favorably. We thought well in excess of estimates, a little bit, I, my understanding is that advertising wasn't quite what management hoped, but they, I thought, had good, a good explanation. I would say Netflix is a high-growth utility. And if you're concerned, the mix of content that people are watching is different than it was a year, five years ago, and that's leading, a calculated time engagement, if you will. But what matters for Netflix is kind of the growth rate of subscribers, the persistency, their ability to price for the enormous value they offer the consumer. We think all those things are extremely strong. You can buy the stock today at one of the lowest valuations in history. And, importantly, I think stock today is something like 18 times earnings. We think the earnings growth here is going to be 20 percent to mid to high teens for the foreseeable future in a, really a utility. Like, to get someone to cancel their Netflix subscription, they have won the streaming wars. I don't know who displaces Netflix. And, yes, they, I think they would like to have some big hits like "Squid Game" and otherwise, and they're making adjustments to the team to make sure that happens, but this is an excellent management team. And I will point out that 18 times earnings today is a similar multiple of cash flow, whereas, four years ago, there was a large gap between earnings and the cash flow of the business. It says the business has matured. It's become enormously cash-flow-positive. I think they bought in something like 3 percent of the outstanding share count, if I got that correct, in the most recent quarter.

EISEN: Yes.

ACKMAN: This is sort of another example of a stock where we will make more money over time if the stock is cheaper in the short to intermediate term because they're going to cancel a lot more shares as a result, so I think another good example of a super high-quality business where a short-term investor is looking—

EISEN: Yes, long term.

ACKMAN: For something to be disappointed about in the quarter outcome, but where we expect our go-forward IRR to be well north of, well into the 20s.

EISEN: Speaking of disappointment in the short term, Fannie and Freddie have been a drag. And I know you have had high hopes that the government, that the Trump administration is going to finally make a move here to privatize. It's taken longer than expected. Did get some comments from Secretary Bessent in a podcast this week saying, I think he said '27 or '28 issue, that they still want to go forward. I would imagine, next year or the year after, we would be tackling the ownership structure. Do you still have high conviction that this is going to happen? Are you still bullish?

ACKMAN: Yes, very bullish. And, actually to point out, our relative underperformance this year in large part is driven by Fannie and Freddie.

EISEN: Yes.

ACKMAN: These are stocks that went from $3 to $15 or so last year and went from $15 to $3 this year. They became fairly sizable positions. We own over well north of 200 million shares of combined companies. So, this was a very big sort of headwind for us. Now, why didn't we sell it at, when the stock was up 5X? Because we, again, believe our view what's going to happen here. Look, actually, what's not talked about, it's actually absolutely politically critical for Fannie and Freddie to be released from conservatorship before the end of the Trump administration. Why is that the case? Because this is an enormously cash-flow-generative asset that, in the hands, for example, of a Democratic administration, could be used in a manner that is politically very threatening to the Republican Party. The control of who gets access to mortgages, and there were, obviously, there were issues during the Biden administration where there were mortgages being granted to people on favorable terms because of skin color and other such initiatives. And it's a tool that can be used in a very political manner. So I, having met with the administration about this topic, I think they view it as absolutely mission-critical it's released, they're both released from conservatorship. We have put forth a very straightforward plan that will get it done more efficiently. Actually, it's really important that the stock is in the hands of institutional investors and is privatized to protect this from becoming a politically controlled asset. That is well understood at the highest levels of the Trump administration. I think the administration toyed with some other alternative approaches to taking these companies public. There was an initiative, I understand, where Fannie and Freddie would be combined under a new holding company. I don't know if you saw the tweet from the president where there's something called the Great American Mortgage Company—

EISEN: Yes.

ACKMAN: Where they, Fannie and Freddie would stay in conservatorship and there would be this new holding company put on top. You know, it is not a viable structure. The simplest outcome here that creates the most value for the American taxpayer is just simply accounting for the $300 billion of payments that have been made to by Fannie and Freddie to the Treasury, fully repaying the $191 billion that was advanced during the financial crisis, and then an uplisting to a major exchange like the New York Stock Exchange. And the president rings the bell, announces a major, hundreds of billions of value creation for the American people, and then he tasks the treasury secretary and Director Pulte with resolving the conservatorship, which is a process, finalizing the capital rules.

EISEN: Yes.

ACKMAN: But what's fascinating to me is, these stocks were $2, $3 dollars a share 14 years ago, when they had no capital and they had no real earnings. And Obama had just basically, with the net worth sweep, taken away 100 percent of their profits forever. Well, since President Trump was first elected and Mnuchin was treasury secretary, he stopped the net worth sweep. These entities have fully rebuilt their capital. What's not, I think, well understood is, Fannie and Freddie today have five times the capital they had historically, 250 basis points or so of capital. They will get to the extraordinary high levels of capital that were initially proposed for Fannie and Freddie by 2030, but we believe the 2.5 percentage points of capital they have today is more than sufficient. It's what Jamie Dimon would call a fortress level balance sheet. I completely understand the treasury secretary when he says that the, first and foremost, the North Star here is, we can't let the change in ownership of Fannie and Freddie in any way affect mortgage rates.

EISEN: Yes.

ACKMAN: And there's no reason why it should. And even the release from conservatorship, the proper process here is, get them to a fortress balance sheet, which is where they are already. You want to add more capital to that, it's just happening sort of naturally. Keep in place the $450 billion of the government backstop in the form of senior preferred, make that backstop something that's paid for. The companies should pay a kind of commitment fee for the backstop, and then you're going to have almost, I would say, a stupid amount of capital. There's no scenario in which these entities would be a threat to the market. I would argue mortgage spreads tighten in that world, because the fear would be, if it's a Democratic administration that wins the next presidential election, I think that creates uncertainty about how Fannie and Freddie are going to be used, what's going to happen with their capital. Are they going to take steps that is going to reduce the underlying mortgage quality? I think all of that can be clarified and resolved. I think it's great that the treasury secretary said '27 or '28. If I were they, I would get busy on this right after the turn of the year and get it done in the 2027 time frame. Now, it's, why do I like these stocks at, why have I held them from $3 to $15 and back to $3? Because, in the scenario I have outlined, these are well into the high $40s, $50 stock. The president has even higher estimates of value.

EISEN: Yes.

ACKMAN: And I think we can get there. What we're saying is just a accounting for the repayment of the preferred, a relisting on the New York Stock Exchange, and these are, these stocks will go up tenfold. And that's a, that's the most asymmetric investment I'm aware of in the stock market.

EISEN: Well, they're spiking now on your comments. But it sounds like—

ACKMAN: We're talking what is an incredibly, yes, incredibly high-quality, these are incredibly high-quality businesses that are trading at like one time's earnings. It's absurd.

EISEN: Yes, well, they have been in conservatorship for 18 years, which is , which is actually hard to believe. Bill, while, while we have you, I just wanted to ask you about Meta.

ACKMAN: Actually, one other point I would make here—

EISEN: Yes, go ahead.

ACKMAN: One other point I would make here with respect to midterms—

EISEN: OK.

ACKMAN: If midterms go against the president, go against the Republicans, that is really going to limit some of what the president can do in terms of things that require approval from the Congress. I mean, the beauty here is, in that world, this is, the Fannie-Freddie release is one of the few things the president can do simply by executive order. We saw, I saw the tweet from Director Pulte agreeing with the treasury secretary on the timing here, is that we got the people that are relevant all in line. This would be a huge victory for the president and a big economic value creation for the taxpayer. So, we remain very bullish here.

EISEN: Yes, clearly. I do, I want to ask you about Meta too, because you're a big shareholder of Meta, and it's down sharply today. It had great earnings, but concerns, I guess, just about how much they're spending. They sort of raised the low end of the CapEx outlook for the year to $135 billion to 145. They're also issuing this, they have this two-for-one split to issue more shares to raise more money, nonvoting shares. I wonder if you have any, any problems with any of this.

ACKMAN: Yes, look, I briefly had a chance, again, on my way on the flight to read the news. Look, California has made, is really heading in the wrong direction. And they're in the process of, I would argue, certainly economically destroying the state. The wealth tax that's been proposed, there's already been a massive flight of people that would be exposed to the wealth tax, so there's no way that it will actually generate the revenues that were originally intended. But, literally, every start-up entrepreneur, I had a meeting yesterday with a start-up entrepreneur in the kind of brain-computer interface space, and they're already making plans to open a New York office, and potentially for the senior management team to leave California because of this tax policy. What, the Meta news, the, at least what was stated in the materials I read is that, if Mark Zuckerberg, if a tax is put in place, he's going to have to sell a large amount of stock in order to pay the tax. And I guess Mark and the board want Mark to remain in control of the company. And by creating a sort of a lower-voting or nonvoting class, this will enable him to do so. This is, I don't, Meta has an incredibly strong balance sheet. They have got $80 billion of cash on the balance sheet. They, they're, they have no net leverage. They could finance whatever they want to do with a very, a turn or two of financial leverage and remain a very strong investment, great company. So this is not a company that's going to have to run out and, look, I think we're in a world in which you cannot look at the day one trading of a stock after earnings because of how levered market participants are and how short-term they are. And they're in a, like, the stock was up when I went to sleep on the flight. It was up something like 5 percent, OK?

EISEN: Yes.

ACKMAN: And I, and when I checked in before this interview, it was down 6.5 percent.

EISEN: We're now down 6.

ACKMAN: These are just short-term traders moving the stock around. I mean, the—

EISEN: But—

ACKMAN: This is a business that is accelerating. You know, Muse is very clearly becoming, is brilliantly designed. I mean, there's some other competitors in the space, but, obviously, Meta is extremely well-positioned—

EISEN: Yes.

ACKMAN: In democratizing the use of agents with this product. They have proven that AI is helping them accelerate their business, and this remains an incredibly undervalued stock, and that's why we own it.

EISEN: It's based a little bit, and I will just ask one finally about what's, what's been the problem lately with the AI trade, which is all the borrowing that's happening. It's continuing to be debt-filled, and we have this, rising interest rates, both market rates and the Federal Reserve, rising rates. There's concerns about the neoclouds and their business models because of how highly levered they are. I mean, do you, do you share some of these concerns about the, I know you're exposed through some of these hyperscalers, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, about just how expensive—

ACKMAN: Yes, I wouldn't—

EISEN: It's going to be in an environment of rising, rising credit costs?

ACKMAN: Yes, so I would say the following. Why are people spending so much money? Because intelligence is one of the most, if not the most valuable asset in the world. And we're asymptotically approaching superintelligence. And the access to compute is critically important for every business model, every company. And I wouldn't question the demand. And why are we playing that demand, owning a Microsoft or an Amazon or even a Meta. The answer is, these are well-capitalized, incredibly dominant franchises that have the balance sheets to make these investments. The neocloud play is a bit like investing in a real estate developer in a highly levered format. And if you get it right, the levered equity returns are enormous. If you get it wrong, you can get wiped out. It's a very different kind of bet. And it's also a bet where they're very sensitive to their, to their cost of capital. And they don't have the market power or the ability to use the compute in the event that demand isn't there. Microsoft and Amazon are going to, and Meta will be able to use every incremental watt, if you will, of compute. And that's why we like their business models versus the neoclouds. But there, there is no question that the demand for compute is enormous. And, by the way, yes, we just I if you look at the SpaceX earnings call—

EISEN: Yes.

ACKMAN: Elon's talking about potentially spending hundreds of billions of dollars on gigawatts of compute. It's clearly -- the demand is there. But, yes, the impact here is, you now have companies like SpaceX and the Mag 7 that are competing with the U.S. government to issue debt, and that's kind of bearish for rates. All that being said, historically speaking, what we have, a 5 percent 10-year is still relatively low cost of capital.

EISEN: You think rates are going higher from here?

ACKMAN: And, by the way, it's a cost of capital, I don't see a world, well, if we can resolve Iran and Russia-Ukraine, I think rates are coming down, inflation's coming down, and that, and, again, that that is, we're off to the races for the economy, the market, and everything else. But the, since intelligence is so valuable, you can earn an attractive return even with a risk-free rate of 5 percent.

EISEN: Well, Bill, we certainly appreciate you taking the time today after a long day in Tel Aviv to talk about the world and your investments and, of course, what you're doing in Israel. So, thank you very much.

ACKMAN: Thanks for having me.
results.title: CNBC Exclusive: Transcript: Pershing Square Founder & CEO Bill Ackman Speaks with CNBC’s Sara Eisen on “Squawk on the Street” Today
